extracted.intended_audience: intellectual property lawyers, in-house counsel, and companies considering or defending Section 337 investigations before the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical procedural and substantive standards for instituting, litigating, and defending investigations under Section 337 of the Tariff Act of 1930 before the U.S. International Trade Commission, with emphasis on patents and other IP-based claims. Covers jurisdiction, pleading sufficiency, domestic industry and injury requirements, remedies, timing, and related tactical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Section 337 / Covered Causes of Action
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 337 'broadly declares unlawful unfair methods of competition and unfair acts in the importation and/or sale of imported articles.' The majority of Section 337 investigations have focused on patent, unregistered trademark, or trade secret claims, and the ITC has accepted jurisdiction over registered trademarks, trade dress, false designation of origin, trademark dilution, copyright (including DMCA), mask work infringement, misappropriation of trade secrets, and various business torts and unfair competition allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 337 was originally a 'catch all' statute but has evolved into an IP enforcement statute. Certain acts (e.g., dumping, unlawful subsidies) are not within Section 337. The Commission looks to general principles/precedents and may consider defenses such as the §271(e)(1) safe harbor where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: In rem jurisdiction and nationwide personal jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 337 investigations are in rem (jurisdiction arises from the importation of products) and the Commission has nationwide personal jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because jurisdiction is product-based, investigation titles list products/processes to provide public notice. In rem jurisdiction permits joinder of domestic respondents from across the country and subjects parties to broad (including foreign) discovery. It also provides a basis for exclusion orders against products irrespective of their source (i.e., general exclusion orders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic industry requirement — two-pronged test (technical and economic prongs)
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain relief a complainant must show that a U.S. industry 'dedicated to the exploitation of the asserted intellectual property rights' exists or is in the process of being established; the requirement has both a technical prong (U.S.-based activities that exploit the specific asserted IP) and an economic prong (significant investment in plant/equipment, significant employment of labor or capital, or substantial investment in exploitation such as engineering, R&D, or licensing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere ownership is insufficient; foreign owners can qualify if U.S. licensees practice the patent. The economic prong can be satisfied by licensing activities, legal fees, and other investments; no bright-line monetary threshold exists. Courts/ALJs examine facts case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical prong of domestic industry — authorization/practice of patent in U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: The technical prong involves whether complainant (or licensees) practice its own patent; activities must be based in the United States and exploit the specific intellectual property rights asserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show that evidence of practice by a licensee or active exploitation in the U.S. supports the technical prong; mere ownership without exploitation fails. The Commission examines the nature and significance of U.S. activities (value-added, manufacturing, licensing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic prong / Substantial investment factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The economic prong concerns investment in domestic industry and can be satisfied by: (1) significant investment in plant and equipment; (2) significant employment of labor or capital; or (3) substantial investment in exploitation (engineering, R&D, licensing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of substantial investment may include number of companies licensed, licensing revenues, licensing costs, employees involved in licensing, legal fees, and whether licensing is active and ongoing. Royalties are an important factor but no minimum monetary expenditure is required; the Commission considers industry context and complainant size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value-added and comparative analysis for domestic-industry assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: When domestic activities are less than all activities exploiting the IP (common in international supply chains), the Commission generally looks to the nature and significance of activities performed in the U.S., often using a comparative 'value-added analysis' to compare foreign vs U.S. value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comparative analysis generally applies to the first two economic tests (investment in plant/equipment and employment) but may not apply to the third test (substantial investment in exploitation), which can be an absolute U.S.-activity inquiry. Examples (e.g., male prophylactic devices) show that significant U.S. value-added by finishing/testing can support domestic industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injury requirement (non-IP claims and nexus test)
rubrics_metrics.description: For non-patent/copyright/mask work/registered trademark complaints, complainant must prove the unfair competition/acts will threaten to or actually: (1) destroy or substantially injure an industry in the U.S.; (2) prevent establishment of such an industry; or (3) restrain or monopolize commerce in the U.S. In all cases, there must be a nexus between the unfair act and the injury to the domestic industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission examines trends in employment, production, capacity, market shares, importation levels, pricing, lost sales, underselling, declining production/profitability. No single factor is dispositive; facts are examined in industry/market context. Federal Circuit has rejected 'conceivable losses' as sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaint sufficiency and pre-institution investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: A Section 337 complaint must contain a substantial amount of detail and supporting exhibits; notice pleading is not sufficient. The Commission conducts a pre-institution investigation (generally ~30 days, longer if a motion for immediate temporary relief is filed) to determine sufficiency and compliance with the Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent-related complaint must support the allegation that the accused imported item or foreign manufacturing process is covered by the asserted patent. The Commission will 'determine whether the complaint is properly filed' and identify sources of relevant information, prepare subpoenas if necessary, then vote whether to institute an investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming respondents and scope of requested remedy (general vs limited exclusion orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kyocera/Broadcom decision: limited exclusion orders under §337(d)(1) apply only to respondents named in the complaint and found to import infringing products; to secure relief covering non-respondent importers a complainant must prove entitlement to a general exclusion order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complainants should name direct importers and downstream importers or seek a general exclusion order with the proof required. Failure to carefully craft respondent list may lead to a remedy different from expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative nature of proceedings — Commission control and role of ALJ
rubrics_metrics.description: Although complaints are typically filed by private parties, Section 337 investigations are instituted and conducted by the Commission. After institution, an ALJ is assigned to preside over discovery, motions, and hearings; the ALJ issues Initial Determinations on liability, temporary relief, summary judgment, or termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within 45 days of commencement the ALJ sets a 'target date' for completion. Initial Determinations become Commission determinations unless the Commission reviews them. With limited exceptions, ALJ decisions on motions cannot be appealed to the Commission prior to an initial determination on violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and status of the Investigative Attorney (IA) / OUII
rubrics_metrics.description: The ITC's Office of Unfair Import Investigations (OUII) provides an Investigative Attorney (IA) who has full party status, participates in discovery, motions, briefings, and hearings, and whose chief roles are to develop a complete record, provide 'objective' advocacy, and safeguard the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The IA cannot engage in ex parte communications with the ALJ, Commissioners, or Office of General Counsel after institution. The IA is an independent third-party participant that can aid or challenge private parties' positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and pace of investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: ITC attempts to complete Section 337 investigations in a very short timeframe (around 12–18 months). The pre-institution investigation generally takes ~30 days; ALJ sets a target date within 45 days of commencement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The accelerated timeline affects discovery, motion practice, and tactical decisions — e.g., costlier complaint preparation and need for early, focused fact development. Motions for immediate temporary relief can extend pre-institution time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary relief / preliminary injunction standards
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining whether to grant temporary relief, the Commission applies the standards used by the Federal Circuit for preliminary injunctions (see 19 C.F.R. § 210.52), which consider irreparable harm, inadequacy of legal remedies, balance of hardships, and public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complainants seeking immediate temporary relief should prepare to meet the preliminary-injunction-like standard and provide supporting evidence during the pre-institution and early stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies available — exclusion orders and cease-and-desist; no damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission's remedies under Section 337 are injunctive in nature and include general exclusion orders, limited exclusion orders, and cease and desist orders; Section 337 remedies do not include damages for unfair acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General exclusion orders can bar importation of infringing products irrespective of source; limited exclusion orders target named respondents. Remedies are subject to presidential review and possible disapproval. The Commission may also enforce orders through administrative mechanisms (see 19 C.F.R. §210.75).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential review and public-interest consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Relief issued by the Commission under Section 337 is subject to disapproval by the President of the United States; public interest considerations factor into the decision and remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, the President has disapproved general exclusion orders where national or industry interests warranted. Parties should be prepared to address public-interest considerations when seeking relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel litigation, mandatory stay of district court proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: GATT amendments permit a respondent who is a party to a district court action to seek a mandatory stay of the district court proceedings for claims involving the same issues as those before the Commission. The stay request must be made within 30 days after being named as a respondent or 30 days after effective service in district court, whichever is later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Princo, the stay continues until Commission proceedings are no longer subject to judicial review (i.e., until finality). After the stay lifts, the Section 337 record may be used by the district court under protective order as permitted by the Rules of Evidence and Civil Procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals to the Federal Circuit — Markman de novo and limits of preclusive effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals from Commission decisions go to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which applies Markman claim construction de novo and can vacate and remand Commission rulings on infringement issues. Commission findings are not binding interpretations of patent law and generally do not have res judicata or collateral estoppel effect in federal courts for patent validity/infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademark adjudications may receive greater preclusive effect. Parties should anticipate Federal Circuit review and possible de novo claim construction in appeals from ITC determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reimported products are subject to ITC jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission has jurisdiction under Section 337 to determine whether the reimportation of allegedly infringing articles (originally manufactured in the U.S., exported, then reimported as finished goods) violates Section 337 and may require issuance of a remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. origin of components does not shield products from ITC investigation. Complainants can seek relief against imported items that contain U.S.-manufactured components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default, abuse of process, and sanctioning standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to participate in the investigation (e.g., failing to provide discovery or respond to pleadings) can result in a default judgment. Section 337 may be dismissed for breach of duty of candor or abuse of process; any party may file a motion for issuance of an initial determination finding a party in default for abuse or failure to cooperate (19 C.F.R. §210.16(b)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission has procedures for addressing defaults and abuses; complainants and respondents should carefully comply with discovery and procedural obligations to avoid sanctions or dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterclaims and removal to district court
rubrics_metrics.description: While counterclaims can be asserted in a Section 337 investigation, they may be 'removed' to the appropriate U.S. district court; antitrust allegations may be considered by the Commission but must not duplicate elements of an antidumping action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should consider strategic implications of asserting or removing counterclaims, particularly where district court jurisdiction or different remedial frameworks (e.g., damages) are sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading and evidentiary standard for patent coverage allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent-related complaint must support the allegation that the accused imported item or foreign manufacturing process is covered by the asserted patent — i.e., there must be adequate detail showing how the accused products/practices fall within the patent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice pleading is insufficient; preparing a Section 337 complaint typically requires more resources than a district-court complaint. Include claim charts, exhibits, and factual support showing literal infringement or doctrine-of-equivalents theories as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: No bright-line thresholds; case-by-case determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Section 337 standards (e.g., what constitutes 'substantial investment' for domestic industry, value-added sufficiency, sufficiency of licensing efforts, degree of injury) lack bright-line tests and are determined on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission and ALJ decisions and Federal Circuit precedent provide guidance, but litigants must assemble fact-specific evidence (financials, licensing records, manufacturing/value-added analyses, market data) to satisfy each element. Documentation quality can be decisive (e.g., 'sweat equity' without detail can fail).
